title: Where does fertilisation happen?
subtitle: Follow sperm and egg in a frog pond and a hen
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: analyse the features of fertilisation in animals, including external and internal fertilisation
lessonIntent: Locate sperm-and-egg joining in named animal examples and explain how supplied conditions affect encounters; distinguish joining inside from later egg laying outside.

authorNotes: One question owns this cut: where sperm and egg join, with conditions that make encounters possible. Hydra budding, haploid/diploid/meiosis, genetic variation mechanisms and detailed parental investment are deferred.
Common frog (Rana temporaria) is the stated external example, not all frogs or all amphibians. Internal fertilisation also occurs in some aquatic animals. Do not classify from habitat alone.
The mnemonic join, shell, lay applies to the hen sequence after its cause is explained, not to every animal reproduction route.

scenes.heading: Both eggs are outside. Did joining happen there?

voiceover.text: A female common frog releases eggs into pond water while a male releases sperm close by. Now look at a hen's egg in a nest. In this example, it is already fertilised. Both eggs are outside the body when we see them. But did sperm and egg join in the same place? To answer, we need to follow the reproductive event, rather than classify an animal from where its egg ends up.

scenes.heading: Follow sperm to the egg in the pond.

voiceover.text: Recall from the previous lesson that sperm and egg are reproductive cells called gametes. Each carries inherited information in DNA. When a sperm joins an egg, we call that fertilisation. It can begin the development of a new animal. In this common-frog example, the female's eggs are already in the pond when sperm reaches them. The joining happens in water outside her body. That makes it external fertilisation. External describes the joining place, not whether the parents live in water.

previewBeats.line: Sperm and egg are reproductive cells.
Fertilisation joins sperm and egg.
previewBeats.spokenCue: When a sperm joins an egg

previewBeats.line: The joining happens outside the female's body.

scenes.heading: Water helps. Sperm still has to reach an egg.

voiceover.text: Why release the gametes close together? A sperm must reach an egg before it can join it. Nearby release shortens that journey. The water keeps these exposed gametes from drying out and provides liquid in which sperm can swim. But water alone does not guarantee a meeting. A current can carry sperm away from the eggs. If the two types of gamete are not present at the same time, they may miss each other too. So a suitable watery setting, a nearby release and overlapping timing support fertilisation in this case.

scenes.heading: The hen keeps the joining place inside.

voiceover.text: The hen uses a different route. Sperm is transferred into the female during mating. Inside her body, it can reach an egg near the beginning of a tube called the oviduct, the passage that carries the egg onwards. Joining there is internal fertilisation. The moist reproductive tract reduces the gametes' exposure to drying, which is useful on land. That protection does not remove the need for sperm to enter the female and reach an egg. The location gives a useful advantage under dry conditions. It does not promise that every egg will be fertilised or that an offspring will survive.

scenes.heading: The nest is a later destination.

voiceover.text: Return to the egg in our opening nest. In a hen, sperm reaches the egg before the hard shell is added. The egg then passes along the reproductive tract, the shell forms around it, and the hen lays it. In our supplied fertilised egg, the joining has already happened inside the body. Later development can continue in the laid egg when conditions support it. For this bird, remember the order: join, shell, lay. That order explains why an egg in a nest does not make fertilisation external. Find the joining place first.

voiceover.text: Try a changed condition. Two groups of common frogs release the same numbers of eggs and sperm into pond water at the same time. Predict how B's opportunities for sperm to reach eggs compare with group A, and explain why. Then name one result these observations cannot tell us. Pause here to decide.

scenes.heading: The joining place stays the same. Encounters change.

voiceover.text: The fertilisation is external because sperm and egg join in pond water outside the female. For B, the stronger current carries sperm away from the eggs, so sperm has fewer opportunities to reach them in the stated comparison. Equal starting numbers do not remove that extra separation. The unchanged viable lifetime, the time gametes remain able to fertilise, does not remove it either. We cannot calculate an exact number of fertilised eggs from these observations. Nor can we predict how many young will survive and later reproduce. The evidence supports a change in meeting opportunities, rather than a guaranteed offspring count.

scenes.heading: Classify the joining place, then explain its conditions.

points: Fertilisation joins sperm and egg. External: outside the female. Internal: inside.
Common-frog example: water limits drying; nearby release at the same time supports encounters.
Hen: join, shell, lay. An egg laid outside can already have been fertilised inside.
